h1:
Getting to Koh Mak
and Around the Island
intro: Koh Mak sits out in the Trat sea, roughly 38 km off the coast. There's no airport on the island, so everyone arrives by boat from a mainland pier. The good news is the island is fairly flat with smooth roads, so you can get around easily on your own by bicycle or scooter. This page covers everything — picking a pier, prices, rough schedules, and how to move around once you land — plus the things you really need to know before buying a ticket.

blocks.html: Koh Mak is the third-largest island in the Trat sea after Koh Chang and Koh Kood, shaped a bit like a four-pointed star and covering nearly 9,000 rai. What people love is that the terrain is fairly flat — none of the steep hills you get on Koh Chang — which makes it much easier to explore on your own. The one thing you have to plan is the boats, because schedules change with the season and some operators stop running during the monsoon.

blocks.text: First step — getting to the pier on the Trat side

blocks.html: Boats to Koh Mak leave from the mainland in Trat province, and there are two main piers to choose from: Laem Ngop Pier (Krom Luang Chumphon) and Laem Sok Pier. Before you reach either one, you first need to travel from Bangkok down to Trat.

items: Driving yourself — from Bangkok, take Motorway 7 then Sukhumvit Road, around 4–5 hours to Trat. There's overnight parking near the piers, roughly 50–80 THB/day.

Minivan / coach — the Transport Co. (BKS) route 999 coach from Ekkamai to Trat is around 290 THB, or there are several minivan departures to Trat each day. Get off in Trat town and continue by songthaew or shuttle to the pier.
Flying — fly into Trat Airport (Bangkok Airways) and continue by road to the pier. It saves a lot of time if you'd rather not do the long drive.
Car + boat package — many boat operators sell combo tickets with a shuttle from Bangkok or Pattaya that arrives at the pier in time for the boat. Handy if you don't have a car.

blocks.title: Give yourself time to catch the boat
blocks.html: Most boats to Koh Mak run from late morning through the afternoon — there are no late-night departures. Coming from Bangkok, you'll need an early start to make an afternoon boat. Aim to reach the pier at least 30–45 minutes before departure to check in and allow for traffic.

blocks.text: Choosing a pier — Laem Ngop or Laem Sok

blocks.html: The two piers differ in crossing time and which operators run from each. Pick whichever has departures that fit your travel timing — prices are about the same either way.

items: Laem Ngop Pier (Krom Luang Chumphon) — the popular one, with several speedboat operators. The crossing is around 45–60 minutes. Good if you want plenty of departures to choose from.
Laem Sok Pier — south of Trat town, with a slightly shorter crossing of around 30–40 minutes. It has both speedboats and catamaran ferries, which ride smoother.

blocks.text: Speedboats vs. ferries — rough prices and schedules

blocks.html: Koh Mak uses two types of boat: speedboats (fast, but you feel the waves more) and catamaran ferries (a little slower but smoother, better if you get seasick). The figures below are approximate high-season prices — check the actual schedule with the operator again before you travel, since timetables often aren't announced far in advance.

items.name: Leelawadee Speedboat
items.blurb: Departs from Laem Ngop — a big, popular operator with several departures a day in high season. The counter is at Krom Luang Chumphon Pier.
items.meta: Laem Ngop · ~45–50 min · to the island late morning–afternoon, back to the mainland morning–late morning

items.name: Panan Speedboat
items.blurb: Another Laem Ngop operator, with afternoon and evening departures — good if you reach Trat in the afternoon.
items.meta: Laem Ngop · ~50 min · evening departure around 16:00

items.name: Boonsiri Catamaran Ferry
items.blurb: A bigger boat that rides smoother than a speedboat, leaving from Laem Sok — good if you get seasick or have a lot of luggage. It also links Koh Chang, Koh Mak and Koh Kood.
items.meta: Laem Sok · ~45–60 min · smooth ride, good for families
tags: Pick this if you get seasick

items.name: Suansuk Speedboat
items.blurb: Runs from Laem Ngop with late-morning and afternoon departures — a solid backup if the other operators are full or don't line up.

items.name: Seatales / The Mak Speedboat
items.blurb: Another Laem Ngop speedboat with departures spread through the day in high season. Call to confirm first, since some months it doesn't run a full schedule.
items.meta: Laem Ngop · ~50 min · confirm departures first

items.name: Slow boat (wooden boat)
items.blurb: A budget wooden boat that takes about 3 hours. It doesn't run every day and departures are very limited — only worth it if you're on a tight budget and genuinely not in a hurry. Check the running days in advance.
items.meta: Laem Ngop · ~3 hours · doesn't run daily

blocks.title: Carry cash
blocks.html: The piers and many spots on the island still take cash only. There are few ATMs on Koh Mak and they sometimes run out of cash, so bring enough to cover boat tickets, your room, vehicle rental and food, with a little extra — better than running short while you're on the island.

blocks.text: What you need to know — the May–Oct monsoon closure

blocks.html: This is the single most important thing to plan around for Koh Mak. The low season, roughly June–October, is monsoon time — strong winds and waves. Most operators cut back to one departure a day, some stop running entirely, and many of the island's hotels and restaurants close for an extended break.

items: Check before every booking — confirm boat departures, accommodation and restaurants are actually open on your travel dates. Don't trust old schedules online.
Have a backup plan — on rough days boats can be cancelled at short notice, so allow for a night stuck on the mainland and have a plan B.

Diving depends on the weather — snorkeling and diving trips around the nearby islands depend on sea conditions. On rough days the water's murky and trips may be cancelled, so don't lock in a fixed plan.
Best window — November–April: calm seas, full boat schedules, and everything open and running.

blocks.text: Once you've landed — how to get around the island

blocks.html: The nice thing about Koh Mak is that it's fairly flat. The loop road around the island is about 27 km, with dedicated bike paths along several stretches, so it's much easier to explore on your own than a hilly island. The main spots — Ao Kao on the west side and Ao Suan Yai on the north — are only a few kilometres apart.

items.name: Scooter rental
items.blurb: The easiest option if you want to loop the whole island. A few stretches of road are slightly steep, where a scooter handles better. You can arrange rentals at the pier, your accommodation, or local restaurants.

items.name: Bicycle rental
items.blurb: A great fit for a flat island like this — easy riding past rubber plantations and sea views, perfect for short hops between beaches. But to loop the full 27 km you'll need the legs and should avoid the midday heat.

items.name: Electric golf cart (EV)
items.blurb: Some accommodations rent out EV golf carts that seat several people — good for families or groups who want to tour the island without sitting in the sun.

items.name: Hotel shuttle / walking
items.blurb: Many resorts run a free or low-cost shuttle from the pier. If you're staying right on the beach and aren't set on looping the island, strolling around the beach is plenty — no rental needed.

blocks.title: Ride safely
blocks.html: Roads on the island are narrow, with sandy patches and slick spots after rain. Wear a helmet, ride slowly, and watch for dogs and chickens crossing. "Petrol stations" on the island are small shops selling fuel by the bottle, so top up before you set off around the island.

items: Pier → Ao Kao — a few kilometres, around 10 min by scooter or 20–25 min by bike.
Ao Kao → Ao Suan Yai — crossing from the west side to the north, around 10–15 min by scooter.
One full island loop — the loop road is about 27 km. By scooter you can take in the sights comfortably in half a day; by bike, allow a full day with rest stops.
Viewpoints / small piers — scattered around the island at short distances, easy to stop and take photos along the way.

blocks.title: Travel light on the island
blocks.html: Koh Mak champions sustainable tourism, and some waste is hard to dispose of on the island. Bring your own water bottle, skip single-use plastics, and carry your trash back to the mainland if you can — it helps keep the island as beautiful as it is.

faq.q: Which pier do boats to Koh Mak leave from?
faq.a: There are two main piers on the Trat side: Laem Ngop Pier (Krom Luang Chumphon), where several speedboat operators run with a crossing of around 45–60 minutes, and Laem Sok Pier, which has both speedboats and catamaran ferries with a slightly shorter crossing of around 30–40 minutes. Choose whichever has departures that fit your travel timing.

faq.q: How much does the boat to Koh Mak cost?
faq.a: Speedboats and ferries run around 450–550 THB per person each way in high season. The budget wooden slow boat is around 200 THB but takes roughly 3 hours and doesn't run every day. Check the actual prices and schedule with the operator again before you travel.

The monsoon low season is roughly June–October, with strong winds and waves. Most boats cut back to one departure a day or stop entirely, and many hotels and restaurants close for an extended break. The best time to visit is November–April, when the sea is calm and everything is open.

faq.q: How do you get around Koh Mak?
faq.a: The island is fairly flat, with a loop road of about 27 km. Scooters are popular at around 250–350 THB/day since they let you cover the whole island, or you can rent a bicycle for around 100–150 THB/day for shorter, relaxed rides. Some accommodations also offer electric golf carts and shuttles from the pier.

faq.q: Do I need to bring cash to Koh Mak?
faq.a: Yes, you should. There are few ATMs on the island and they sometimes run out of cash, and many shops and services still take cash only. Bring enough to cover boat tickets, accommodation, vehicle rental and food, with a little extra — better than running short while you're on the island.
